analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the repeal of the federal estate tax on large inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: introduced January 7, 2003, it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a markup or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law eliminated the estate tax, but only through 2010, after which it was scheduled to come back. This bill would have struck that expiration date, making the repeal permanent. The estate tax only applies to very large inheritances, so the benefit would flow almost entirely to the heirs of the wealthiest estates, while the federal government would permanently forgo billions of dollars a year in revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates — in practice, families with multi-million-dollar fortunes — would keep more of their inheritance, since the estate tax touches only estates above the exempted amount. Estate planning attorneys, wealth advisors, and the financial industry also benefit, since repeal removes the need for estate-tax planning (though many had already built businesses around minimizing the tax while it existed).

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the sunset provision of the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001 as it applies to estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, so the estate tax would never come back after 2010 [S2][S3].

For the small share of families whose estates are large enough to be taxed, permanence means certainty in planning — the exemption and zero rate would be locked in rather than returning after a decade [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays, in the form of revenue permanently forgone. That cost lands on everyone else — as deficits, lower public spending, or higher taxes elsewhere — because the bill provided no replacement revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue offset; it permanently removes estate tax receipts that the 2001 law only temporarily suspended, adding to federal deficits [S2][S3].
The estate tax by design applies only to very large estates, so repeal is a targeted transfer to the wealthiest households at a cost to the general budget rather than a broad-based tax cut.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated: only a small fraction of estates are large enough to owe any estate tax, and those owe it on inheritances measured in millions. The cost is diffuse — billions a year in lost federal revenue borne by all taxpayers. An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill is a wealth transfer dressed as a repeal, while an honest opponent would concede it does simplify planning for a small set of families.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it sat until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott McInnis introduced the bill on January 7, 2003 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No further action was taken — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the 108th Congress expired on January 3, 2005, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the federal Treasury kept the estate tax revenue that would have been permanently forgone, and the cost stayed with general taxpayers rather than being shifted through deficits. The narrow group that would have gained — heirs of the largest estates — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; the estate tax survived

for.name: Rep. Scott McInnis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2001 estate tax repeal permanent; it was referred to Ways and Means and went no further [S5].

for.name: 1 House Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only support it attracted beyond its sponsor [S4].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chair Bill Thomas
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on January 7, 2003 and took no action — no markup or vote — leaving it to die when the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the record shows only two Republican members supporting it (the sponsor and one cosponsor) and no recorded opposition, so the partisan shape of the bill's fate cannot be measured from the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: Permanent repeal would have eliminated a tax paid only on very large inheritances, a direct gain for the families holding the country's largest fortunes. The cost — lost federal revenue — would have been spread across all taxpayers. The bill's death preserved the status quo. Sources: [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory services
industries.note: Repeal would have shrunk demand for estate-tax planning, but wealth managers also stood to gain as clients inherited larger untaxed sums. The tax's survival preserves a large compliance and planning industry built around it. Sources: [S3].
